title: Image Layers, Tagging, and Pushing
intro: An image is just a stack of cached layers, and a tag is just a pointer to one — understanding both is what makes rebuilds fast and deployments predictable.

steps.prompt: See the layer history of the 'myapp:v1' image, including how big each layer is.
steps.fake_output:
IMAGE          CREATED BY                                      SIZE
i9j0k1l2       CMD ["node" "server.js"]                        0B
a1b2c3d4       COPY . .                                         1.2MB
e5f6g7h8       RUN npm install                                 180MB
z9y8x7w6       FROM node:20-alpine                              45MB
steps.explanation: That 180MB npm install layer is the expensive one — if you COPY source code before running npm install, every code change invalidates the cache and forces a full reinstall.
steps.why: This is exactly why Dockerfile instruction ORDER matters: put things that change rarely (installing dependencies) before things that change often (copying source code), so Docker's layer cache can skip the expensive step on most rebuilds.

steps.prompt: Tag the existing 'myapp:v1' image as 'myregistry.io/myapp:v1' to prepare it for pushing.
steps.explanation: This doesn't copy or rebuild anything — it just adds a second name pointing at the exact same image layers.
steps.why: Docker decides where to push an image based entirely on the registry hostname prefix in its tag — an image tagged just 'myapp:v1' has nowhere to push to, which is why re-tagging with the full registry path is a required step before push, not optional.

steps.prompt: Log in to the registry before pushing.
steps.explanation: Credentials get cached locally after this, so you don't need to log in again for every subsequent push in the same session.
steps.why: Skipping this and going straight to push against a private registry gets you a plain 'unauthorized' error — the same failure mode as incident-006 (ImagePullBackOff) in the Kubernetes tutorials, just on the push side instead of the pull side.

steps.prompt: Push the re-tagged image to the registry.
steps.fake_output:
The push refers to repository [myregistry.io/myapp]
a1b2c3d4: Pushed
e5f6g7h8: Pushed
v1: digest: sha256:abc123... size: 1234
steps.explanation: Only layers the registry doesn't already have get uploaded — if a previous version shares base layers with this one, those are skipped.
steps.why: This is the same layer-caching concept from 'docker history' applying again, just over the network this time — it's why pushing a small code-only change is fast even for a large image, since only the changed layer(s) actually transfer.

steps.prompt: Clean up local disk space by removing images that have no container using them and aren't tagged.
steps.explanation: This only removes 'dangling' images — layers left behind from old builds that no tag points to anymore.
steps.why: This is scoped to images specifically, a narrower version of 'docker system prune' — reach for this one when you just rebuilt an image several times and want to clean up the intermediate leftovers without touching stopped containers or networks too.
